slides.say: Two congruent circles, with centers O and M, touch each other from the outside. Each one has a radius of seven centimeters. M A and M B are tangent to the circle with center O, at A and B. What is the smaller angle A O B?
We need an angle, but the only number we have is a length, the radius seven. [short pause] Let's use the math way. We start from the givens and see what each one gives us.

M A and M B are two tangent segments to the circle O, from the same point, M. Remember, two tangent segments from the same point to the same circle are equal. And together with the radii to the points of tangency, they make a kite.
at: two tangent segments from the same point

slides: But right now there's no kite in the drawing, because the radii aren't there. So let's add a helper line, a radius to each point of tangency. We draw it because it gives us right angles.

slides.say: So let's draw the radius from O to A, and from O to B. Both are seven. A radius to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, so we get ninety degrees at A, and ninety at B.

Now we have a kite. Its angles add up to three hundred sixty. Ninety plus ninety is one hundred eighty, so the angles at O and at M share the other one hundred eighty. But we can't split it yet, so it's still not enough.
[pause] There's a given we haven't used. The two circles are congruent, and they touch each other. To use the touching, we join the two centers, O and M.
at: There's a given we haven't used

slides.say: When two circles touch from the outside, the touching point lies between the centers, on the line O M. So the first part of O M is a radius of circle O, seven. The second part is a radius of circle M, and the circles are congruent, so it's seven too. So O M is seven plus seven, which is fourteen.
at: So the first part of O M
So O M is seven plus seven

slides.say: Compare that with circles that touch from the inside. The small circle is inside the big one, and they share one touching point. Draw both radii to that point. They overlap along the same straight line. The part between the centers is the big radius minus the small radius. With radii five and two, the distance between the centers is five minus two, three. In our question the circles touch from the outside, so we add the radii, seven plus seven.
at: They overlap along the same straight line

slides.say: [pause] Now look at the right triangle O A M. One leg, O A, is seven, and the hypotenuse, O M, is fourteen.
at: Now look at the right triangle
One leg, O A, is seven

slides: Here the hypotenuse is twice a leg, fourteen and seven. That's the gold triangle ratio we know. In the gold triangle, thirty, sixty, ninety, the sides are x, x root three and two x. So its hypotenuse is twice the short leg. The silver triangle doesn't fit here, because its hypotenuse is the leg times root two.

slides.say: So O A is the short leg, and the angle across from it, at M, is thirty degrees.
The lower triangle, O B M, is the same triangle, so the angle at M there is thirty too. This time we went backwards, from the sides to the angle.
[pause] In each gold triangle, the angles are thirty, sixty and ninety. The thirty is at M and the ninety is at A, so the sixty is at O. It's the same in both triangles.
at: so the sixty is at O

slides.say: Angle A O B is made of the two angles at O, one from each triangle. So angle A O B is sixty plus sixty, which is one hundred twenty. Choice number three is our answer. Sixty, choice number one, is only half of the angle.
at: So angle A O B is sixty plus sixty
Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: You can also finish with the kite. The angle at M is thirty plus thirty, which is sixty. The kite's angles add up to three hundred sixty. Three hundred sixty minus ninety and minus ninety is one hundred eighty. And one hundred eighty minus sixty is one hundred twenty. The same answer.
at: You can also finish with the kite
The angle at M is thirty plus thirty
eighty minus sixty is one hundred twenty

slides: So again, what did we do? We used two types of helper line. First the radii to the points of tangency, which gave us right angles. Then the line between the centers, which used the touching circles. And we spotted a gold triangle from its sides. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
